A halo is a circle of light placed above or around the head of a holy figure, honouring their sanctity. Countless Middle Ages and Renaissance paintings depict notable figures this way, and the imagery leads viewers to judge those figures favourably. The halo effect works the same way. One obvious trait leads an observer to a broader, unfounded conclusion about the whole person (Ellis, 2018). A single positive quality can create a positive predisposition toward every other aspect of that person. One negative attribute can do the reverse. The positive version is the halo effect; the negative version, covered later, is the horn effect. The halo effect is also not a stereotype. It generalises from one trait of an individual, whereas a stereotype applies generalisations to a whole group. The “what is beautiful is good” stereotype sits where the two overlap. Swapping “polite” for “blunt” made little difference. - Conclusion: Impressions are not a simple sum of separate traits. Central traits like warm-cold organise the whole impression and spread to unrelated qualities, which is the process that drives the halo effect. Asch also found a primacy effect: the same adjectives produced a more favourable impression when the positive ones came first. The Reverse Halo Effect The horn effect is the halo effect’s mirror image: one negative trait unduly darkens the whole impression, so a single flaw overshadows real strengths. The reverse halo effect, also called the horns effect, is a cognitive bias. A negative overall impression of a person darkens perception of their specific, unrelated traits. It is the opposite of the halo effect, where a positive impression leads to positive perceptions. The reverse halo effect works the same way in miniature. Negative traits overshadow positive qualities, producing biased judgments and evaluations. For instance, the horn effect may lead us to stereotype an overweight person as lazy. The halo effect is sometimes used to refer specifically to when this behavior has a positive correlation, such as viewing someone who is attractive as likely to be successful and popular. When this judgment has a negative connotation, however, such as when someone unattractive is more readily blamed for a crime than someone attractive, it is sometimes referred to as the horn effect.[16] Marketing [edit] The term halo effect is used in marketing to explain consumer bias toward certain products because of favorable experience with other products made by the same company.[17] It is used in the part of brand marketing called "line extensions." One common halo effect is when the perceived positive features of a particular item extend to a broader brand. A notable example is the manner in which the popularity of Apple's iPod generated enthusiasm for the corporation's other products.[18][19] Advertising often makes use of television shows, movies and those who star in them, to promote products via the halo effect.[20][21]

passages.text: Halo effect The halo effect (sometimes called the halo error or halo fallacy), a term coined by Edward Thorndike, is the tendency for positive impressions of one aspect of a person or entity to encourage a positive perspective on that subject's other aspects.[1][2] It is "the name given to the phenomenon whereby evaluators tend to be influenced by their previous judgments of performance or personality;"[3] in other words, it is a cognitive bias that can prevent people from forming an image based on the sum of all circumstances at hand. A simplified example of the halo effect could be when people, after noticing that an individual in a photograph is attractive, well groomed, and properly attired, then assumes, using a mental heuristic based on the rules of their own social concept, that the person in the photograph is a good person.[4][5][6] This constant error in judgment is reflective of the evaluators' preferences, prejudices, ideology, aspirations, and social perception.[7][6][8][9][10] Context and applications [edit] Psychology [edit] The term halo effect is used in psychology to describe a perception distortion that affects the way people interpret the information about others with whom they have formed a positive gestalt.[11] For example, they find out

It is the most-cited demonstration of the effect. - Aim: Dion, Berscheid and Walster (1972) tested whether physical attractiveness triggers a halo. They asked whether good-looking individuals are also assumed to have better personalities and life prospects. - Method: Participants were shown photographs of people pre-rated as attractive, average or unattractive. They judged each person’s traits and predicted marital happiness, career success and overall life satisfaction. - Results: Attractive people were credited with more desirable personalities, such as being kinder and more interesting, and with happier marriages and more prestigious jobs. Few areas favoured the unattractive group. - Conclusion: Physical attractiveness sets off a broad halo: the “what is beautiful is good” stereotype. One visible trait inflates judgements of unrelated qualities, and even predictions about a stranger’s future. In the Classroom In the classroom, teachers are prone to the halo effect error when evaluating their students. A teacher might assume a well-behaved student is also bright and motivated. That judgement often comes first. It arrives before they have objectively evaluated the student’s actual ability. Clifford

One desirable-sounding attribute inflates judgements of the product’s calories, quality and healthiness, even when that inference is unwarranted. Shoppers under-estimate calories or over-consume. It is the “what is beautiful is good” logic applied to food rather than to people. Marketers engineer halos deliberately. A strong “hero” product lifts expectations for a company’s whole range (Ries, 2006). Attractive, likeable spokespeople work the same way: consumers transfer positive feelings about the endorser onto the brand. A well-known brand can charge a premium because its reputation substitutes for direct evidence about the item in front of the shopper. Origins of the Halo Effect The American psychologist Frederick L. Wells (1907) gave an early hint of the halo effect. Judges rating the literary merit of authors produced suspiciously uniform ratings. However, it was Edward Thorndike who first recognized it with empirical evidence. Thorndike was an early behaviorist who delved into the psychology of learning. He officially introduced the term ‘the halo error’ in 1920 in his article, “A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings”. Evidence Check: Does the Halo Effect Hold Up? Verdict: Supported with qualifications. The core finding holds: a global evaluation leaks into judgements of unrelated qualities. The evidence is strongest for physical attractiveness and for ratings of job performance, each backed by meta-analysis. The mechanism is less settled. The size of the halo also depends on what is being judged. Three claims are weighed: - Asch’s central traits: A rerun found no primacy of warmth. Experiment; not yet replicated. - The attractiveness halo: Real but moderate, and content-specific. The object can leach some metallic properties into the soil, making it more detectable. The area surrounding the object is called its "halo." The observer may be subject to overestimating the worth of the observed by the presence of a quality that adds light on the whole, like a halo. In other words, observers tend to bend their judgment according to one patent characteristic of the person (the "halo") or a few of his traits,[46] generalizing toward a judgment of that person's character (e.g., in the literal hagiologic case, "entirely good and worthy"). The effect works in both positive and negative directions (and is hence sometimes called the horns and halo effect). If the observer likes one aspect of something, they will have a positive predisposition toward everything about it.
